# The Weight of What He Saw

Tariq is a 41-year-old man who came to the United States from Lebanon twelve years ago, carrying with him the hope of a quieter life. For most of those years, he managed to find something close to that — a small apartment, a steady job at a fast food restaurant where he has worked the morning shift for the past six years, and a routine that felt, if not joyful, at least manageable. That sense of steadiness collapsed eighteen months ago on a Tuesday afternoon when he watched a man get struck and killed by a delivery truck in the parking lot directly outside the restaurant's front windows.

Tariq was standing at the counter when it happened. He saw the whole thing — the truck, the impact, the man's body on the ground, the stillness that followed. He remembers the sound most of all. He describes it in a way that is quiet and precise, the way a person describes something they have replayed thousands of times without wanting to. He was the one who called 911. He stayed until the paramedics arrived, because it felt wrong to leave, and then he went back inside and finished his shift because he did not know what else to do.

He did not sleep that night, or the night after. In the weeks that followed, he told himself he was fine — that he had seen difficult things before, growing up during periods of violence in Beirut, and that this was no different. But it was different in a way he could not quite name. The man in the parking lot had looked at him through the window in the seconds before the truck came. Tariq is not certain of this, but he believes it. That belief has become something he cannot put down.

Now, a year and a half later, Tariq moves through his days with a vigilance that exhausts him. At work, he positions himself away from the front windows whenever possible. When a delivery truck pulls into the lot — which happens several times each week — he feels his chest tighten and his hands go cold. Sometimes he has to step into the back and stand near the fryer, staring at nothing, waiting for the feeling to pass. His coworkers have noticed that he is quieter than he used to be, though no one has asked directly.

He does not drive anymore. He tells people it is because he does not own a car, which is technically true, but the real reason is that being near moving vehicles on open roads produces a dread he cannot control. He takes the bus, and on the bus he sits near the back and watches the street through the window with an attention that is less curiosity than surveillance.

At night, he sleeps in fragments. The dreams are not always about the accident — sometimes they are about Beirut, about things he thought he had filed away — but they carry the same texture of helplessness, the same sense that something terrible is already in motion and cannot be stopped. He wakes at three or four in the morning and lies still, listening to the sounds of the building around him, unable to distinguish between what is safe and what is not.

He has stopped calling his sister in Beirut as regularly as he used to. When she asks how he is, he says he is busy with work. He does not want to explain, partly because he does not have the words in Arabic for what is happening to him, and partly because he suspects she would tell him he has seen worse, which is true, and which would not help.

What strikes him most, sitting in the office and speaking haltingly about all of this, is that he does not feel like himself anymore. He describes the person he was before as someone who could stand at a window without flinching. He is not sure how to get back to being that person, or whether that is even possible.
